question: In recent years we have been witnessing a growing number of Italian and European doctors and healthcare workers leaving for the Middle East and the Gulf countries, especially Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. These countries invest around 10% of their GDP in healthcare. Estimates show that, since May 2022, 800 doctors, 600 nurses and 250 physiotherapists and osteopaths left Italy for Saudi Arabia.

One of the reasons healthcare professionals are moving to these countries is that they offer much higher salaries that European countries do, as well as numerous benefits. In addition, the rising population in Middle Eastern and Gulf countries is creating a growing demand for well-trained specialists.

In light of this exodus of highly qualified professionals, a veritable brain drain, can the Commission say whether it is concerned about this trend and, if so, what steps does it intend to take to curb it, bearing in mind that, in the long term, this situation could put national healthcare systems in European countries under serious strain?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.4.2024) The Commission acknowledges that labour shortages in the healthcare sector are of concern to Member States and, in particular, that the health workforce faces a challenging working environment related to working conditions.

According to Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union1, Member States are responsible for the management of health services, including the allocation of resources to ensure the sufficient availability of the health workforce.

The Commission supports Member States in strengthening the health workforce through several actions, including a Joint Action on forecasting and planning of health workforce2, five projects on workforce retention, task shifting and medical deserts3, actions on skills development under the BeWell project4, training projects focusing on digital skills5 and a new action addressing shortages of nurses6.

In addition, following the Social Partner Summit in Val Duchesse on 31 January 2024, the Commission has put forward an Action Plan on tackling labour and skills shortages to highlight the need for joint efforts in concerned sectors, including the healthcare sector. Other EU funding instruments such as the Cohesion Policy Funds and the Recovery and Resilience Facility can support complementary actions.
The Italian recovery and resilience plan supports the modernisation of the health system through reforms and investments. In particular, Investment 2.

2 of Mission 6 Component 2 is aimed at investing in skills and training of national health service (NHS) personnel, and includes, inter alia, the financing of additional 2 700 scholarships in the general medicine training with the objective of increasing the number of general practitioners as from 2024.
